config.title: Build timeout and cancellation for HTTP clients

intro.title: Build timeout and cancellation for HTTP clients
intro.body: In this lesson, you will build a simple HTTP client in Node.js that can set a timeout to automatically cancel requests that take too long. You'll learn how to use the built-in `fetch` API along with the `AbortController` and `AbortSignal` to implement request cancellation. This will help you manage network reliability by preventing your application from hanging indefinitely on slow or unresponsive servers. By the end, you'll have a practical understanding of handling timeouts and graceful error handling in HTTP communications.
intro.usecase: Timeout and cancellation for HTTP clients is essential in any production Node.js application that communicates with external services. In e-commerce platforms, this prevents checkout processes from hanging indefinitely when payment gateways are slow. API dashboards use timeouts to ensure slow third-party data providers don't freeze the entire interface. Search autocomplete features implement cancellation to discard outdated requests as users type, while file upload services need timeouts to handle network interruptions gracefully.

objectives: Configure HTTP client timeout settings using the built-in Node.js modules
Implement request cancellation logic with AbortController and AbortSignal
Construct error handling mechanisms for timeout scenarios
Integrate timeout and cancellation features into existing HTTP client code
Manipulate request parameters to include timeout and abort signal options
Apply timeout patterns to both GET and POST HTTP requests
Initialize multiple concurrent requests with individual timeout controls

steps.title: Import required Node.js modules
steps.instruction: Import the http and https modules from Node.js core using the require() function.
steps.hint: Use the require() function to import built-in Node.js modules. No need to install them separately.
steps.seedCode: // Import http and https modules here
steps.expectedOutcome: The http and https modules are imported and ready to use for making HTTP requests.
successCriteria: The http and https modules are imported using require() statements.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track. Make sure you're importing both http and https modules.
steps.feedbackWrong: Check that you're using require() to import both http and https modules from Node.js core.

steps.title: Create a basic HTTP request function
steps.instruction: Create a function named 'makeRequest' that takes a URL string as a parameter and uses the http module to make a GET request.
steps.hint: Define a function with the name 'makeRequest' and a single parameter (e.g., 'url'). Inside, you'll use http.get() to initiate the request.
steps.expectedOutcome: You'll have a function named makeRequest that accepts a URL parameter, ready to contain HTTP request logic.
successCriteria: A function named makeRequest is defined with a url parameter.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've created the basic request function structure.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure the function is named exactly 'makeRequest' and takes a 'url' parameter.
steps.feedbackWrong: The function isn't defined correctly. Check the function name and parameter.

steps.title: Add timeout parameter to the request function
steps.instruction: Modify the makeRequest function to accept a timeout parameter as its third argument.
steps.hint: Add a third parameter named 'timeout' to the function definition. You can set a default value (like 5000) to make it optional.
steps.expectedOutcome: The makeRequest function should now have three parameters: url, options, and timeout.
successCriteria: The makeRequest function accepts a timeout parameter as its third argument.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you've added a timeout parameter to the function definition.
steps.feedbackWrong: The timeout parameter hasn't been added correctly. Check the function signature.

steps.title: Implement timeout logic with setTimeout
steps.instruction: Inside your makeRequest function, create a setTimeout that will abort the request if it takes longer than the timeout value. Store the timeout ID in a variable so you can clear it later.
steps.hint: Use setTimeout with the timeout value from options. Inside the callback, you'll need to abort the request (you'll implement that in the next step).
steps.expectedOutcome: Your function should now have a setTimeout that triggers after the specified timeout duration.
successCriteria: The makeRequest function contains a setTimeout call that uses the timeout value from options.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure the setTimeout uses the timeout value from the options parameter.
steps.feedbackWrong: The timeout logic isn't implemented yet. Add a setTimeout inside makeRequest that will trigger after the timeout duration.

steps.title: Handle timeout cleanup
steps.instruction: Inside your makeRequest function, clear the timeout timer when the HTTP request completes successfully (either on 'response' or 'error' events).
steps.hint: Use clearTimeout() with the timer reference you created earlier. Place this cleanup inside the event listeners for the request.
steps.expectedOutcome: The timeout timer will be properly cleaned up when the request finishes, preventing memory leaks and unexpected behavior.
successCriteria: clearTimeout() is called inside the request's completion event handlers.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure clearTimeout() is called in both success and error cases of the request.
steps.feedbackWrong: The timeout cleanup is missing or incorrectly placed. Remember to clear the timeout when the request finishes.

steps.title: Add error handling for timeout events
steps.instruction: Inside the makeRequest function, add error handling that rejects the promise with a timeout message when the timer fires. Use the setTimeout callback to reject with a descriptive error.
steps.hint: In the setTimeout callback, call reject with a new Error containing a message like 'Request timed out after X ms'.
steps.expectedOutcome: The makeRequest function should now handle timeout events by rejecting the promise with an appropriate error message when the timeout occurs.
successCriteria: The setTimeout callback inside makeRequest rejects the promise with a new Error containing a timeout message.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure the setTimeout callback properly rejects the promise with a descriptive Error object.
steps.feedbackWrong: The timeout error handling isn't implemented correctly. Check that you're rejecting the promise with an Error in the setTimeout callback.

steps.title: Wire timeout to trigger cancellation
steps.instruction: Inside the setTimeout callback in your makeRequest function, call abortController.abort() to cancel the request when the timeout occurs.
steps.hint: The abort() method on the AbortController instance will trigger cancellation. Call it inside the timeout callback function.
steps.expectedOutcome: The timeout mechanism will now properly cancel ongoing HTTP requests when they exceed the specified duration.
successCriteria: The setTimeout callback includes abortController.abort() call to cancel the request.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you're calling abort() on the AbortController instance inside the setTimeout callback.
steps.feedbackWrong: The timeout isn't properly triggering cancellation. Remember to call abortController.abort() inside the setTimeout callback function.

steps.title: Create a test function to demonstrate timeout
steps.instruction: Create a function named testTimeout that calls makeRequest with a URL and a very short timeout (e.g., 10ms) to demonstrate timeout behavior.
steps.hint: Define a function that invokes makeRequest with a URL like 'http://example.com' and a timeout value small enough to trigger a timeout error.
steps.expectedOutcome: A testTimeout function is defined that will call makeRequest with a short timeout, allowing you to see timeout behavior in action.
successCriteria: The testTimeout function is defined and calls makeRequest with a URL and a timeout parameter.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure your testTimeout function actually calls makeRequest with both a URL and a timeout parameter.
steps.feedbackWrong: The testTimeout function is missing or doesn't properly call makeRequest with a URL and timeout. Try defining a function that invokes makeRequest('http://example.com', { timeout: 10 }).

steps.title: Test manual cancellation functionality
steps.instruction: Inside your testTimeout function, add a test case that demonstrates manual cancellation by calling abort() on the AbortController after a short delay.
steps.hint: You can use setTimeout to call abort() after a few milliseconds, then verify the request is cancelled.
steps.expectedOutcome: The testTimeout function will include a demonstration of manual cancellation separate from timeout-based cancellation.
successCriteria: The testTimeout function contains code that calls abort() on an AbortController instance to manually cancel a request.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you're calling abort() on the AbortController instance within the testTimeout function.
steps.feedbackWrong: The manual cancellation test isn't implemented correctly. Review how to create an AbortController and call its abort() method.
